title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 23
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A recycling centre introduced a booking system for visits and reports that the queue at its entrance has disappeared. The council concludes that the centre now serves residents better.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The booking system is operated through a website.
B. Staff find the site easier to manage.
C. Fly-tipping in the surrounding area rose sharply, and residents without internet access report being unable to obtain slots.
D. The centre is open six days a week.
E. Bookings can be cancelled without penalty.
questions.explanation: The queue was removed by rationing access, and the displaced disposal plus the excluded residents are costs the queue measure does not see.

questions.prompt: A golf club raised its annual subscription and reports that its income from subscriptions rose. The committee concludes that the club could raise the subscription further with similar results.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The club has a long waiting list.
B. Subscriptions are paid annually in advance.
C. Neighbouring clubs charge more.
D. The members who resigned after the increase were disproportionately those who used the bar and restaurant, and revenue from those has fallen by more than the subscription gain.
E. The course was improved in the same year.
questions.explanation: Total revenue fell even though the subscription line rose, so extrapolating from the line that improved is unsafe.

questions.prompt: An office installed air conditioning and reports that staff productivity, measured by tasks completed per hour, rose during the following summer. Management concludes that cooling the office improved productivity.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How much the air conditioning cost to install
B. How the previous summer's temperatures compared with those of the summer measured
C. Whether staff were consulted about the installation
D. How many staff work in the office
E. Whether the system is serviced regularly
questions.explanation: A cooler summer would produce the same result without the equipment; without the comparison the effect cannot be attributed.

questions.prompt: A publisher notes that books selected by a popular book club sell far more copies than books that are not selected, and concludes that selection by the club causes high sales.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the publisher's conclusion?
options: A. In a period when the club chose its selections by lot from a shortlist, the chosen titles outsold the unchosen shortlisted titles by a similar margin.
B. The club has many members.
C. Club selections are announced in advance.
D. Selected books are displayed prominently in shops.
E. Some club members buy books they do not read.
questions.explanation: A lottery among comparable candidates removes the possibility that the club simply picks books that would have sold anyway.

questions.prompt: Every product sold at the Marden farm shop that carries the county food mark is produced within twenty miles. No product produced within twenty miles is transported by refrigerated lorry. Some products sold at the shop are transported by refrigerated lorry.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. The county food mark guarantees freshness.
B. Most products are produced within twenty miles.
C. Refrigerated transport is more expensive.
D. Products carrying the mark are more popular.
E. Some products sold at the shop do not carry the county food mark.
questions.explanation: Refrigerated products are not produced within twenty miles, and the mark implies that they are, so those products do not carry it.

questions.prompt: A museum opened a café and reports that visitors now stay 40 minutes longer on average. The director concludes that the café has increased engagement with the collection.
questions.question: The reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. ignores the revenue the café generates
B. does not distinguish between weekday and weekend visitors
C. relies on estimates rather than measurements
D. treats time spent on the premises as time spent with the collection
E. assumes the café is profitable
questions.explanation: The additional time may be spent sitting with a coffee, which is a fine reason to open a café but not evidence about engagement.

questions.prompt: A city fitted secure bicycle parking at its railway station and reports that recorded bicycle thefts at the station fell by 70 per cent. Officials conclude that the parking has reduced bicycle theft in the city.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the officials' conclusion?
options: A. Thefts from residential streets within a mile of the station rose by a comparable number over the same period.
B. The secure parking requires a monthly subscription.
C. The parking has space for two hundred bicycles.
D. Some cyclists continue to use the old racks.
E. Bicycle sales rose in the city that year.
questions.explanation: Displacement leaves total theft roughly unchanged, so the station-level fall does not support a city-level claim.

questions.prompt: A restaurant group reports that kitchens led by chefs trained in its own apprenticeship have lower food waste than kitchens led by externally recruited chefs, and plans to fill all head chef posts from its apprenticeship.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Apprentices are paid less than external recruits during training.
B. The apprenticeship lasts three years.
C. Apprentice-trained chefs are given the group's simplest menus, which use fewer perishable ingredients, while external recruits run the seasonal restaurants.
D. Some apprentices leave the group after qualifying.
E. Food waste is measured by weight.
questions.explanation: Menu assignment explains the waste difference, so the comparison measures the kitchens rather than the chefs.

questions.prompt: A home care service reduced the standard length of a visit from 30 minutes to 20 and reports that it now serves 40 per cent more clients with the same staff. Managers describe this as an efficiency gain.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the description?
options: A. Care workers travel between visits.
B. Emergency call-outs and hospital admissions among clients rose sharply, and the tasks left undone in the shorter visits are recorded as the reason.
C. Clients were informed of the change.
D. Some visits had previously finished early.
E. The service employs both full-time and part-time staff.
questions.explanation: Work and cost moved into other parts of the system, so more visits delivered is not the same as more care delivered for less.

questions.prompt: A supplier argues that its new packaging is more sustainable, since it uses 30 per cent less material than the packaging it replaces.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: A. The new packaging is a different colour.
B. The new packaging costs less to produce.
C. Customers have not commented on the change.
D. The supplier ships to several countries.
E. The new material cannot be recycled in existing facilities, while the old packaging was recycled at high rates.
questions.explanation: A claim about sustainability must cover the whole life of the material; less input with no recovery route can be worse overall.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to move a town's weekly market from Saturday to Wednesday argue that it will reduce congestion, since Saturday traffic is heaviest. Opponents reply that most market traders depend on weekend shoppers.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply?
options: A. Some traders attend markets in several towns.
B. The market has operated on Saturdays for a century.
C. Wednesday parking charges are lower.
D. In three comparable towns that moved their markets midweek, trader takings were unchanged after six months, as regular customers shifted their shopping day.
E. The council would not charge traders more for a midweek pitch.
questions.explanation: Evidence from comparable moves addresses the mechanism the reply depends on — that the customers are tied to the day rather than to the market.

questions.passageText:
Standard theory expects prices to adjust continuously to changes in cost and demand. Observed prices do not: many firms change them once or twice a year, and hold them through conditions the theory says should move them. The explanations offered have shifted over time, and the shift is instructive.

The first explanation was administrative. Changing a price costs something — reprinting, reprogramming, notifying customers — and small adjustments are not worth those costs. Surveys of managers found this real but minor. Firms reported that the paperwork was rarely what stopped them.

What managers reported instead was the customer relationship. Raising a price in response to a cost increase invites a buyer to reconsider the whole arrangement, including whether to look elsewhere, and a firm with long-standing customers is reluctant to open that question over a small amount. Prices are therefore adjusted in infrequent steps and are noticeably stickier downward in some markets and upward in others, depending on which direction threatens the relationship.

Two consequences follow that matter beyond the firm. If prices adjust slowly, a change in monetary conditions affects quantities before it affects prices, which is the mechanism by which such changes have real effects at all — a piece of microeconomic detail that carries much of macroeconomics. And a firm holding a price will adjust something else instead: package size, delivery speed, the quality of what is supplied. Measured inflation captures the price and often misses the rest, which means the recorded figure understates the change a customer actually experiences.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, surveys of managers found administrative costs of changing prices to be
options: A. the principal obstacle to price adjustment
B. real but minor, and rarely what stopped them
C. larger than economists had estimated
D. irrelevant in every industry studied
E. confined to firms with printed catalogues
questions.explanation: The passage reports the explanation shifted from administrative costs to the customer relationship for this reason.

questions.passageText:
Claims about animal intelligence have a long history of overstatement followed by correction, and the corrective tradition is as important as the discoveries.

The founding case is a horse that appeared to perform arithmetic and was shown, by careful testing, to be responding to unconscious movements made by its questioner. The lesson was not that the horse was unintelligent — reading a human's posture that finely is a considerable feat — but that the ability demonstrated was not the one claimed. Every subsequent claim has had to exclude the same possibility.

Modern work is designed accordingly. When corvids were reported to bend wire into hooks to retrieve food, the significant feature was not the behaviour itself but the controls: novel materials, no opportunity to observe a demonstration, and experimenters who could not cue the animal. Where such controls are weakened, effects shrink, and several widely reported findings in primate cognition have not survived replication under stricter conditions.

The interpretive difficulty remains. An animal solving a problem may be reasoning about it, or applying a rule learned by association, and behaviour alone frequently cannot distinguish these. The productive response has not been to choose a side but to design tasks where the two predict different actions — which is slow, produces smaller claims than the headlines, and is the reason the securely established findings are narrower and more interesting than the popular ones.
questions.prompt: The case of the calculating horse is presented as showing that
options: A. animals cannot perform arithmetic
B. careful testing is rarely possible with animals
C. unconscious cueing is a modern discovery
D. the horse was of unusual intelligence for its species
E. the ability demonstrated was not the ability claimed
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly notes that reading posture that finely is itself a considerable feat.

questions.passageText:
Money sent home by workers abroad exceeds official development assistance to many countries, and is more stable than either aid or private investment, because a migrant's obligation to family does not fluctuate with market sentiment. Remittances typically rise when the home country suffers a shock, which makes them insurance of a kind no formal scheme provides.

The effects at household level are well documented and largely positive: higher consumption, more schooling, better nutrition, and greater ability to absorb an emergency. The effects at national level are more contested. Large inflows can raise the exchange rate and make other exports less competitive; remittance income may reduce pressure on governments to improve services; and the emigration producing the flows removes workers, often those with training the country paid to provide.

The accounting on that last point is not straightforward. Emigration of skilled workers is a loss, but the prospect of emigration also raises the return to acquiring skills, and some who train in the hope of leaving do not leave. Whether the net effect on a country's skill stock is negative depends on rates the available data measure poorly.

What can be said with more confidence concerns the cost of transfer. Fees on small remittances have historically consumed a substantial share of the amount sent, falling on precisely those least able to bear them, and reductions in those fees deliver benefits that are immediate, measurable, and unusually uncontroversial by the standards of this debate.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, remittances function as insurance because they
options: A. typically rise when the home country suffers a shock
B. are guaranteed by receiving governments
C. are paid in foreign currency
D. exceed official development assistance
E. are exempt from transfer fees
questions.explanation: A migrant's obligation does not fluctuate with market sentiment, unlike aid or investment.

questions.passageText:
The claim that photography freed painting from the obligation to record appearances is the standard account of nineteenth-century art, and like most standard accounts it compresses something more interesting.

The mechanical part is true enough. Portrait miniaturists lost their trade rapidly, and the demand for topographical views and family likenesses moved to the camera. But painting had not been solely a recording technology, and painters had been moving away from descriptive finish before photography was commercially available, for reasons internal to painting.

What photography changed more profoundly was the standard against which a picture was read. Once anyone could see what a horse's legs do in mid-gallop, painted gallops that contradicted the evidence became errors rather than conventions. And once mechanical accuracy was cheaply available, accuracy alone ceased to be a distinction, which shifted value toward what the camera then could not do: colour, scale, duration, the visible trace of a hand.

Photography also supplied painters with material. Painters used photographs as references, worked from them for poses that could not be held, and absorbed compositional habits — the cropped figure, the accidental arrangement — that the camera made familiar. The influence ran both ways, since photographers spent decades arranging their pictures to look like paintings. The useful formulation is not that one medium displaced the other but that each altered what the other could take for granted.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that painters had begun moving away from descriptive finish
options: A. only after photography became commercially available
B. in response to the loss of the miniature trade
C. at the request of photographers
D. before photography was commercially available, for reasons internal to painting
E. when colour photography appeared
questions.explanation: This is the passage's main qualification of the standard account.
